books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012 (radio stations and household ownership)

stimulus.text:
Radio in the United States, 1922–1930:

| Year | Licensed radio stations | Homes with a radio |
| 1922 | about 30 | fewer than 1 in 100 |
| 1923 | about 570 | 1 in 100 |
| 1930 | 618 | 40 in 100 |

Source: Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7 (almost 600 licensed stations by 1923); Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012 (stations and household ownership); “Radio in the United States” (1 percent of homes in 1923).
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7; Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012; and “Radio in the United States.”

source: original; stimulus table compiled from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.7, and the Proceedings of the IEEE, 2012
stem: The growth shown in the table most directly helped create

options.text: a national audience hearing the same programs
a return to local newspapers and town meetings
options.misconception: Radio pulled people toward national programs, not back to town meetings. Local papers kept going, but radio was the new shared medium.

options.text: a ban on advertising over the airwaves
options.misconception: Radio advertising grew in the 1920s; stations sold airtime, and ads became standard.

options.text: a sharp fall in the price of radios
options.misconception: Radios got cheaper as sales grew, but the table shows growth in stations and homes, not prices. The question asks what the growth created.

rationales.A: With hundreds of stations, the same programs could reach listeners across the country at the same time. Radio built one national audience.
rationales.B: Radio pulled people toward national programs, not back to town meetings. Local papers kept going, but radio was the new shared medium.
rationales.C: Radio advertising grew in the 1920s; stations sold airtime, and ads became standard.
rationales.D: Radios got cheaper as sales grew, but the table shows growth in stations and homes, not prices. The question asks what the growth created.
rationales.general:
1. Note what the table measures: stations and homes with radios, both rising fast.
2. Ask what hundreds of stations make possible: the same program at the same hour, everywhere.
3. Name the result: one national audience, hearing the same shows and news.
4. Check the scale: by 1930, 40 homes in 100 had a radio, so the audience was truly national.
Remember: when a medium spreads everywhere, ask what people start to hear in common.
